task: On R1, create or select subinterface 20 of GigabitEthernet0/0 for the VLAN 20 gateway design.

teaching.hint: Select a logical subinterface of the existing physical parent.
teaching.takeaway: The .20 suffix is a local identifier. It does not bind traffic to VLAN 20; the encapsulation command must specify the VLAN separately.

task: You are in R1 Gi0/0.10 subinterface configuration. Bind it to traffic tagged for VLAN 10.

teaching.hint: The tag association belongs on the router subinterface.
teaching.takeaway: The encapsulation VLAN is what selects tagged traffic, not the subinterface suffix. Configure the association before assigning the gateway address.

task: You are in R1 Gi0/0.99 subinterface configuration. The switch sends native VLAN 99 untagged; associate this subinterface with that untagged VLAN.

teaching.hint: The native keyword changes how the specified VLAN is carried.
teaching.takeaway: This must agree with the switch trunk’s native VLAN. An unused native subinterface need not receive an IP address merely because it exists.

task: On DSW1, both correctly addressed SVIs are up and hosts reach their own gateways. IPv4 routing is disabled. Enable forwarding between the connected VLANs.

teaching.hint: SVI addresses alone do not enable the multilayer switch’s routing function.
teaching.takeaway: The routing function allows packet forwarding between appropriate interfaces. Verify the connected routes and both traffic directions; a gateway ping alone proves only local reachability.

task: VLAN 10 already exists on DSW1. Create or select its logical SVI so it can receive a gateway address.

teaching.hint: The Layer 2 VLAN object and its Layer 3 interface are separate.
teaching.takeaway: An SVI also needs addressing and administrative enablement. With normal autostate, the VLAN must be active and have an eligible linked, forwarding member.

task: DSW1 Gi1/0/24 supports routing and is selected. Convert it from a Layer 2 switchport into a physical routed interface.

teaching.hint: Change the interface role before assigning a Layer 3 address.
teaching.takeaway: A routed port is separate from an SVI and does not belong to an access VLAN. Configure and verify its address and operational state separately.

task: SW2 is a non-routing access switch. Its working management SVI is 192.168.99.10/24; use reachable router 192.168.99.1 for SW2’s own off-subnet traffic.

teaching.hint: Configure the non-routing switch’s gateway, not inter-VLAN forwarding.
teaching.takeaway: This serves traffic originated by SW2. It does not make the switch route users between VLANs; a routing-enabled switch instead uses its routing table.

task: Vlan10 has an address but hosts cannot reach it. Display the SVI’s detailed interface state and hardware address.

teaching.hint: Inspect the logical interface named for the VLAN.
teaching.takeaway: Read both interface and line-protocol state. If the SVI is enabled but not operational, check VLAN existence and an eligible forwarding member before changing the IP address.

task: After enabling the gateway interfaces, display only the directly connected IPv4 routing entries to check their subnet prefixes.

teaching.hint: Filter by the connected route source.
teaching.takeaway: A connected entry should match the intended subnet and gateway interface. Its presence is local routing evidence; it does not prove the remote host’s return path.

task: After converting DSW1 Gi1/0/24 into a routed port, display its switchport view to verify that Layer 2 switchport operation is disabled.

teaching.hint: Verify the role change on the exact physical interface.
teaching.takeaway: Look for Switchport: Disabled. This confirms the interface role, while address and link-state checks establish whether the routed connection can operate.
